name: Tinder Elo

lead: Tinder Elo is the belief that the dating app assigns each profile a hidden desirability score, modelled on the Elo rating used in chess, and shows profiles to people with similar scores. Within looksmaxxing communities it is a way of thinking about why some profiles get many matches and others few.

The appearance payoff comes through photos and presentation: if better pictures draw more right swipes from desirable users, the score is said to rise. Tinder's CEO described an Elo-style score in 2016 reporting, and the company said in 2019 that it no longer relies on Elo.

paras: Community methods include making a fresh account, limiting swiping sessions, being selective about right swipes, switching settings between searches, and using new, higher-quality photos. Forum members disagree on whether any of these change outcomes.

There is little physical risk. Reported downsides are time spent, disappointment when methods do not change match counts, and privacy considerations when using VPNs or multiple accounts, which can conflict with app terms.

chain: More right swipes from users who are themselves frequently liked
angle.text: Forum users treat the supposed score as a reason to improve photos, grooming and swiping habits, expecting better profiles to be shown more often and to more desirable users. How Tinder ranks profiles today is not published in detail, so the photo advice rests on how members expect the system to behave.

lead: Tinder Elo is a community term for a supposed hidden attractiveness or desirability score that Tinder uses to decide whose profiles are shown to whom. The name comes from the Elo rating system created by Hungarian-American chess master and physics professor Arpad Elo, which adjusts a rating up or down depending on the rating of the opponent beaten or lost to.[1]

Looksmaxxers discuss it because it links appearance directly to dating-app visibility: the idea is that photos and swiping behaviour raise or lower the score, so better photos, grooming and presentation lead to being shown to more attractive users and more matches. Looksmax.org threads describe attempts to boost or reset the score, and a commercial photo-rating site that publishes advice on the topic presents profile photos as the main lever.[2][3][4]

Unlike many looksmaxxing concepts, the idea has a documented origin in the company's own words. Tinder chief executive Sean Rad described an Elo-style desirability score to Fast Company in early 2016, according to Engadget and The Next Web, and in a March 2019 blog post the company said Elo was outdated and no longer used, adding that matching relies on recent activity, preferences and location.[5][5][6]

paras: The Elo rating system estimates relative skill: a player's rating rises when they beat a higher-rated opponent and falls when they lose to a lower-rated one, and a 100-point advantage corresponds to roughly a 64 percent expected score.[1] The United States Chess Federation adopted it in 1960 and FIDE in 1970, and it has since been adapted to tennis, football, video games and esports among others.[1] Wikipedia notes that Tinder reportedly uses a variant.[1]

In the Tinder version of the theory, being swiped right by people with high scores raises your own, while being swiped left by them lowers it, and profiles are shown mainly to others of similar rank. A looksmax.org method thread describes it as a ranking based on right-swipe proportion and recommends selective swiping and periodic account resets, crediting the technique to a user on another forum.[2] A guide published by the photo-rating service Photofeeler describes scores as starting high at sign-up and settling as people swipe on a profile, and advises testing photos, using the app regularly and being selective rather than swiping right on everything.[4]

Tinder was prototyped by Sean Rad and Joe Munoz in early 2012 under the name MatchBox, launched on the iOS App Store in September 2012 and reached Android in July 2013; co-founders include Justin Mateen, Whitney Wolfe Herd and Jonathan Badeen, and the swipe mechanic was modelled on a deck of cards.[7] Matching is double opt-in: two users must like each other before they can message.[7]

Wikipedia cites a 2016 study finding that men liked a large share of profiles but matched only rarely, while women were more selective and matched at higher rates, which is the pattern looksmaxxers refer to when they discuss why match counts differ between men.[7] Tinder data from 2018 showed about 26 million matches from 1.6 billion daily swipes.[7]

In November 2015 Tinder announced a new matching algorithm. TechCrunch reported that CTO Ryan Ogle said machine learning "assesses and interprets the signals" sent by users, and that Rad declined to confirm whether the app analyses photos for traits, saying he could not reveal it.[8]

In January 2016 Fast Company reported Rad describing an internal "Elo score" based on desirability and inspired by chess rankings; The Next Web relayed his comment that the score was not only a tally of right swipes and that "a lot of factors go into it", and that he likened the system to a game of Warcraft.[6] According to Engadget, Tinder product vice president Jonathan Badeen made a similar comparison, saying that playing someone with a high score gains you more points, meaning a like from a more desirable user who liked you back raised your score.[5]

In March 2019 Tinder published a post saying Elo was an outdated measure its technology no longer relies on; it said matching uses recent activity, preferences and location, that each like or pass can change a profile's recommendations within about 24 hours, and that it does not store data on race or income.[5] Engadget noted that the new system still depends on who swipes on whom, that Tinder did not explain how, and that the company said it rewards people who use the app more, which the outlet suggested could favour engagement and revenue from paid features such as Boosts and Super Likes.[5]

sections.h: Beliefs and methods in the community
paras: The best-known method thread on looksmax.org, relaying a technique originally posted on another forum, says dating apps are Elo-based and that the account holder should make a new account, show himself to both men and women, and swipe only occasionally; replies in the thread include a short dismissal and a reply asking him to elaborate.[2] The thread's author frames this as a "hack" for later travel.[2]

Another thread asks how to fully reset the score on a phone, with the poster saying he wants to use a VPN to access Tinder in the United States; replies are mostly jokes.[9] In the community, resets are discussed via new accounts, VPNs and deleting the app, and members disagree on whether any of this has an effect.

The topic overlaps with photo optimisation: because the claimed route to a higher score is a stronger profile, forum members and commercial photo-testing services recommend better lighting, clear solo photos and testing images with raters.[4]

One poster on looksmax.org argued that Tinder Elo does not exist, reporting steady matches after swiping only on women he rated highly, and that low matches reflect competition from many attractive men.[3] Others in the same thread replied that the effect becomes visible with longer use, and the original poster said he had seen the same matches on a stay in another country several months earlier.[3]

No studies found. A 2016 study of Tinder use in New York City and London, summarised on Tinder's Wikipedia article, found men liked a large share of profiles but matched about 0.6 percent of the time, while women were more selective and matched at a higher rate.[7] No published study has tested whether swiping behaviour or account resets change a profile's placement.
